needsYou.title: Your sign-in page is a fixed light screen whatever theme the app is in - deliberate, or just old?
needsYou.productImpact:
Nothing is broken and nobody has complained. This is a taste question about the first page a customer sees, and one sentence from you decides it.

The app has a dark theme and a light one. The sign-in page has neither: it is painted with 116 fixed colour values and knows nothing about the theme. So a customer using Drape in dark mode who signs out - or follows an email verification link - lands on a full-brightness white page. The verify-email page does the same.

That may be exactly right. A deliberately bright front door is a real choice and plenty of products make it. But nothing anywhere in either file says it was chosen - it is simply how things were painted before the theme existed, and never revisited. Found while sweeping the staff pages, which were rebuilt off this same pattern earlier this week.

Either answer is small. The wrong guess means repainting your front door twice.
needsYou.workedExample: You are in dark mode, you sign out, and the screen goes white. That is what happens today. The only question is whether it should.

options.label: Deliberate - the front door stays light
options.consequence: A line in the file recording that it is a decision, and the two pages marked as a known exception to the colour rule. Nothing a customer sees changes.

options.label: It should follow the theme like everything else
options.consequence: The two pages move to the house colours - the four values map cleanly, so it is small - then looked at in both themes before it ships, with your eye on the result.

needsYou.recommendation: No recommendation on this one, deliberately: it is a look-and-feel call about your own front door and either answer is defensible. Whichever you pick, the two pages stop being invisible to the colour rule, which is what they are today.

needsYou.title: A picture you have answered but not finished with: should it wear the same badge a card does?
needsYou.productImpact:
A small look-and-feel question, and it is yours because it is about pictures.

When you answer a card on this page but the job is not finished, it keeps a badge - ANSWERED, STILL YOURS TO DO - so it stays in front of you instead of quietly disappearing. That was your own instruction: keep it on your desk until the act is done.

The same state can now apply to a set of FRAMES in your gallery, and there the badge is not drawn. So a picture you have already ruled on looks exactly like a fresh one waiting for you.

The cheap answer is to put the same badge on the gallery. The reason nobody has just done it: frames are judged by looking, and a badge sitting on top of a picture may read as clutter where the same badge on a card reads as information. That is a taste call, not an engineering one.

WHAT WE WOULD DO IF YOU SAY NOTHING: leave the gallery alone. It is the smaller risk - a gallery item you have answered still shows your reply underneath it, so nothing is lost, and a picture stays a picture.

Everything else on that card is built and merged; this is all that is left of it.
needsYou.workedExample:
You open the gallery in the morning. Two sets of frames sit there. One you looked at last night and ruled on - the answer is recorded, but the change it asks for has not landed yet, so it is still technically yours. The other you have never seen.

Today they look identical. You have to open the first one and read your own reply underneath it to remember that you already dealt with it.

On the CARDS above, that same situation is labelled: a small badge reading ANSWERED, STILL YOURS TO DO. The question is only whether a picture wants the same badge or is better left clean.

options.label: Put the same badge on gallery items - one rule, both places
options.consequence: One rule in both places, so nothing you have ruled on can look fresh again. The cost is a small label sitting on top of a picture you are being asked to judge by eye.

options.label: Leave the gallery clean - a picture is judged by looking at it
options.consequence: The gallery stays as clean as it is now. Your reply is still shown under each set of frames, so nothing is hidden - you just have to read it to remember you answered.

needsYou.recommendation:
Leave it, unless it has already annoyed you. The badge earns its place on a card because a card is a wall of words and the badge is how you find your place in it. A frame is a picture, and anything printed over it competes with the thing you are being asked to look at. Your reply is already shown underneath each set of frames, so nothing is actually hidden today.

One word either way closes it.

needsYou.title: When you answer something and the next step is still yours, it leaves your desk
needsYou.productImpact:
This page sorts what you see into 'needs you' and 'already dealt with'. A card moves to 'already dealt with' the moment you REPLY to it.

Most of the time those are the same thing. They come apart in one shape, and it is the worst possible one: you answer the question, and the remaining step is ALSO yours - you said yes, and now something needs you to flip a switch, run a thing, or look at a picture. At that exact moment the card leaves your desk and files itself under 'no action needed'.

A WORKED EXAMPLE, and it is a real one: a card asked you to approve a shape. You did. Its remaining step was one command only you could run. It vanished off your desk into history the second you engaged with it, and it sat there.

The cheap half is already fixed - pictures put here for your eyes no longer disappear before you have looked. What is left is your call on the shape.

THE ASK: should a card you have answered, but that still needs an act from you, stay in 'needs you' as its own visibly different kind - or would you rather it went back to looking like a fresh ask? The first is more honest and adds a fourth kind of card to this page. The second is simpler and slightly blunter.

RECOMMENDATION: the first. You should never have to go looking in 'already dealt with' for something that is waiting on you. Nothing is blocked by this - it had been sitting with nothing saying it needed you, which is the fault that turned it up tonight.
needsYou.workedExample: A card asked you to approve a shape. You said yes. Its remaining step was one command only you could run - and the moment you replied, the card left 'What needs you' and filed itself under 'Already dealt with'. It sat there, looking finished, with the only person who could finish it never seeing it again.

options.label: Give it its own kind - it stays on your desk, visibly different from a fresh ask
options.consequence: Nothing you have answered can hide in history while it still needs you. Adds a fourth kind of card to this page, so there is one more thing to glance at - but it is the only option where 'needs you' actually means needs you.

options.label: Send it back to looking like a fresh ask
options.consequence: Simpler, nothing new on the page, and it still gets in front of you. But it loses the fact that you already answered once, so it reads as if we forgot you replied - which is its own small insult.

needsYou.recommendation: The first. You should never have to look in 'Already dealt with' for something that is waiting on you, and this page's whole job is that split being true.

needsYou.title: The plan panel: the wrong-plan fault is fixed, and one imprecision is left
needsYou.productImpact:
Change plan tells somebody how fast they are spending, when they will run out, and which plan fits them. Until tonight all three came from the credits an account has spent IN ITS WHOLE LIFE, divided by the days elapsed in ONE month.

That was not only a wrong sentence. The same number picks which plan gets the single dark Upgrade button. On a test account ten days into a month it chose Studio at $159 where the truthful reading chooses Pro at $68 - a $91-a-month upsell built on a claim about the customer's own usage that was not true. Nobody was ever shown it, and that is luck rather than design: the panel only draws once an account has a real billing period, and none has one yet. It would have gone live silently on your first subscription.

That is fixed and merged. What is left is smaller and is why this card is open: a billing period starts at a TIME OF DAY, and the usage figures the panel adds up are kept in whole days. So the first day of a cycle can carry a few hours of the previous one - the spend reads slightly high, and on day two of a cycle that is most of the figure. It is bounded, it needs a change on the server rather than on the screen, and it is written down as its own job.
needsYou.workedExample:
Same account, same moment, ten days into a 30-day cycle with 20,000 credits left.

Before tonight:

    At this rate you run out on 9 Sept.
    120,000 of 140,000 spent... Studio covers the way you are actually working.
    [ the dark Upgrade button on Studio, $159 / month ]

Now:

    At this rate you run out on 13 Sept.
    40,640 of 60,640 spent... Pro covers the way you are actually working.
    [ the dark Upgrade button on Pro, $68 / month ]

Both pictures are in your gallery below. The remaining imprecision would move that 40,640 by at most one day's spending.

options.label: Fix the remainder properly - ask the server for the period's spend
options.consequence: One new read on the server, at the exact times rather than in whole days. Removes this and a related 90-day limit at once. Half a shift.

options.label: Leave it - it is at most one day out
options.consequence: Nothing to build. The panel stays slightly generous about spend on the first day or two of a cycle, and the note stays on the record.

options.label: Nothing tonight, and take the frames as read
options.consequence: The card waits. The merged fix is live either way.

needsYou.recommendation: (a), but not urgently - it is the last member of a family that has now produced three separate wrong numbers on your money screens, and closing it removes the whole shape rather than another instance. The frames below need thirty seconds of your eye whatever you choose, because that panel is the last thing somebody sees before they pay us.

needsYou.title: One of your seven plan lines makes promises the other six do not
needsYou.productImpact:
Six of the seven lines you approved only say who a plan is FOR - "For a team shooting a campaign a month." Nothing the product does can make a sentence like that untrue.

The Free line is the exception: "Try the studio. A few casts a month, no card." That promises roughly how much someone gets, and that no card is needed. Both are true today.

The risk is narrow but it sits on a billing page. If you ever cut the free allowance or start asking for a card at signup, that line silently becomes a false claim to every visitor, and nothing in the product would warn us - no test can read English well enough to notice.

It has been left exactly as you approved it, because it is your copy and changing your words to suit a note of ours would be the worse mistake. Instead it is written down in two places, and the test now pins that line word for word so nobody quietly rewrites it without reading why.

Today:

    Try the studio. A few casts a month, no card.

The same line in the shape the other six use:

    For trying the studio out before you commit.

The credits block directly underneath already says exactly what they get, so nothing is lost by dropping the promise from the sentence.

needsYou.title: A safety prompt on the six commands that can destroy work has a way around it - one minute of your hands
needsYou.productImpact:
Your settings file puts six git commands behind a confirmation prompt. They are the destructive family - the ones that can throw away work nothing can give back - and two of them act on whatever folder they are run in, including the working folder your own sessions share with the night shifts.

The prompt matches on how the command starts. There is a second, perfectly ordinary way to write those commands - naming the folder first - and written that way they match none of the six patterns, so they run with no prompt at all. A shift measured this after hitting it by accident doing something legitimate. Nothing has been lost. The point is that nothing would have stopped it.

It is on your desk rather than fixed because it lives in a file no shift may edit - and more to the point, a session editing the permission file that governs it is the one edit that should never be automatic.
needsYou.workedExample:
Measured, three ways of writing the same command:

    git merge origin/main                -> asked (correct)
    cd <folder>; git merge origin/main   -> asked (correct)
    git -C <folder> merge origin/main    -> RAN, no prompt

The same shape is git -C <folder> reset --hard, which destroys uncommitted work in that folder. The fix is adding the second spelling of each of the six to the same list - about a minute. The card carries the exact lines.

options.label: Add the six second spellings
options.consequence: The prompt covers both ways of writing the command. No effect on anything routine - these are spellings of commands you already chose to be asked about.

options.label: Leave it
options.consequence: The prompt stays easy to walk around by accident, on exactly the commands that can lose work.

needsYou.recommendation: (a). While you are in that file, card #571 asks for a related narrowing in the same place, so the two are one sitting.

needsYou.title: Deploy on merge is built and waiting — three fields in Railway flip it (#508)
needsYou.productImpact:
Today nothing you merge actually ships until the deploy script runs on your machine — a merged fix can sit invisible for hours, and every deploy routes through one laptop. The design you ordered is now decided and built: after your flip, **merging is shipping.** The moment a PR lands on main, Railway builds it and it goes live — no laptop, no ceremony, no waiting.

Two safety nets went in first, and both are already active the next time we deploy: a new build that cannot start healthy **never takes traffic** (customers keep getting the old, working version), and database tables now create themselves **before** the new code goes live instead of after, on every road. Rolling back stays one click in Railway, or one revert merge.

One thing to know, said plainly: after the flip, a merge landing while you are mid-roll can still cost you the known ~6-minute wait (money always conserved). The polite hold-while-you-work check stays on the nightly record pushes, and a follow-up card (#585) adds the same manners to the way shifts merge.
needsYou.workedExample:
In Railway → Drape service → Settings, in this order:
1. **Pre-deploy command**: `node dist/predeploy.js` (timeout 600). This rehearses safely on the current road first — the next deploy proves it in the logs before anything depends on it.
2. **Healthcheck path**: `/api/health`.
3. **Watched branch**: change `local-migration` to `main` — this is the flip.
Then reply 'flipped' and a shift arms the watcher (a GitHub setting), retires the old branch, and runs the proof from the card: one trivial merge watched going live with no script, one revert watched going live the same way.
needsYou.recommendation: Flip it when you have five quiet minutes. Steps 1 and 2 rehearse safely on the current road first, step 3 is the switch, and rollback stays one click in Railway either way.

needsYou.title: Your tail court ran, and your premise did not reproduce — I need your word before chasing the reason (#530)
needsYou.productImpact:
You ordered one last check before closing the species sentence: your sphinx-cat brief, two arms of eight, with the sentence and without, both strips in front of you. It ran tonight for $1.56 of house money — no credits of yours, nothing on production.

THE TAIL LANDED ON ALL 24 FRAMES, on both arms. I could not make your brief fail.

Two things follow from that, and the first is good news about your sentence. It is not what puts the tail there — and it never was on THIS brief. The house instruction has always had two parts, and only the second one is yours: an older line already says that anatomy the description NAMES must be visible in the frame, and your sentence covers the case where a part is NOT named. Your brief names the tail. So both arms carried the older line, and both grew tails. Your sentence is neither proved nor disproved by this brief — and it is shown to do no harm, which was the other thing worth knowing.

The second thing needs you. You said the brief 'has never once rendered the tail', and I believe you — but I drove a different road than you did. This court sends your words straight to the engine with the house instruction attached. The frame you sent me came from a Re-imagine roll, where a writer rewrites your brief first. If that rewrite softens or drops 'long tail' on the way past, the house instruction has nothing left to hold on to, because by then the description is the writer's and not yours.

That is a different fault on a different road, and I stopped rather than chase it, because it touches the thing you are about to judge.

Whiskers, on your own three counts: 7 full + 1 small, then 6 full + 2 small, then 8 full — which leans the way your sphynx-breed hunch predicted, but one frame in eight is not a difference and I will not dress it as one. No clause is being added to the house instruction on that reading, exactly as you instructed.

needsYou.title: Your "optimize it as urgent" is built, all five pieces — the verdict is the only thing left, and it is yours (#543)
needsYou.productImpact:
You asked, on the 5th: "investigate our current process and optimize it as urgent." The investigation found the team sitting idle for 52% of a typical night — 27 minutes of every session waiting on automatic checks with nothing else on the bench. Five things were ordered off that finding and all five are now built, tested and in use:

  1. a shift checks its own work before it asks the machines (about 100 seconds instead of a 7-minute red)

needsYou.title: You ruled the audit — five move, not six, and the one you held back has its answer
needsYou.productImpact:
ANSWERED, and you changed the split in a way the measurement agrees with.

FIVE MOVE, not six: the modal shell, the destructive confirm, the overflow menu, the rename dialog and the delete-by-typing ceremony. The brief text box you held back.

YOUR HELD QUESTION IS ANSWERED, and the answer is not the one the question expected. You asked whether promoting casting's text box would make a third input implementation, since the shared kit already has Field and Input. It would not — they are not the same kind of thing. Field is a wrapper box that holds a label and an input; Input is a one-line text field; casting's is a MULTI-LINE box, and the shared kit has no multi-line box at all. It already borrows Input's own styling and adds eight lines on top. So it is the missing sibling rather than a rival.

BUT YOUR INSTINCT WAS RIGHT, ONE LAYER OVER. There ARE duplicates here, and they are the popover situation again: THREE different boxes in the product grow as you type, and THREE guard against a Japanese, Chinese or Korean customer pressing Enter to finish a character — and casting's is the only one that does both. That second thing is a money control: on the casting page Enter spends 160 credits, so a customer committing their characters would buy a roll they did not ask for.

So: casting's survives and is promoted as the shared kit's missing multi-line box, and the two OTHER grow-as-you-type copies are what needs reconciling — not Field. That is a separate piece of work and it is written down rather than started.

AND THE DROP-ZONE CHECK YOU ASKED FOR LATER, TAKEN NOW: you are right, the shared kit already has one and the upload card does not use it. The eventual work is smaller than the audit assumed.

eyeItems.title: One switch for the whole panel — and the page you cited as correct was never doing it either
eyeItems.question:
You asked why the refresh controls act as individual toggles per admin page, and said it should work the way the moderator pages work. It does now. But the reason it was broken is not the reason it looked broken, and that decided the fix.

THE MODERATOR PAGE WAS NEVER SHARING ANYTHING.

It looks like it holds the switch across everything you do because /moderator is ONE page — its tabs are inside it, so nothing ever unloads. The admin panel is EIGHT separate pages, and each one loaded a fresh switch set to off. Neither side had any shared setting at all; seven pages each kept their own private copy. So copying the moderator page would have been copying nothing. What has been built is the thing neither side had.

WHAT YOU SHOULD SEE.

Turn AUTO 30s on anywhere — Overview, Users, Change requests, Invite codes, Bug reports, Audit logs, or the moderator dashboard — and walk anywhere else. It is on. Turn it off and that travels too. Close the browser and come back tomorrow and it is still how you left it.

⚠ ONE DECISION IS YOURS, AND I HAVE MADE A CALL YOU MAY WANT TO REVERSE.

One shared switch means one starting position, and the eight pages disagreed about it: Overview started ON, the other seven started OFF. I looked up why Overview was different, expecting a decision of yours — it was not. It came from the original scaffolding commit back when that page was first built, so nobody ever chose it.

I have set the shared starting position to ON, because that way no page loses anything it did today and you get what you asked for without clicking. The cost is that five admin pages now re-read themselves every 30 seconds when they used not to. The alternative is OFF, where nothing starts polling that did not before, but your landing page stops refreshing on arrival the way it always has.

Either way it remembers you the moment you touch it, and it is one line to flip. Say the word if you want OFF.

THE FRAMES BELOW ARE THE SAME PAGE, NOTHING CLICKED.

Both are /admin/users reached by clicking Users from Overview. On the left of each pair is how it is now, on the right how it was this morning.

eyeItems.title: The missing refresh controls — and your question found twice what the card did
eyeItems.question:
You asked why only some admin pages carry "the updated time the auto refresh toggle and a notification button". They all do now. But the interesting part is what turned up on the way, and it is worth two minutes.

THE CARD SAID TWO PAGES WERE WRONG. FOUR WERE.

Whoever wrote the card searched the pages for the setting that draws those controls and found two pages missing it — Invite codes and Bug reports. That search was answering a slightly different question than yours. Users and Change requests HAD the setting, and inside it they had only the refresh button — no time, no toggle. So they matched the search and still failed two of the three things you named. The first frame below is the Users page as it was: one lonely refresh icon and nothing else.

THE REASON THOSE TWO PAGES GAVE FOR IT WAS SIMPLY WRONG.

Each had a note in the code saying the missing pieces were "state no reader produces" — meaning the page had nothing to show, so showing nothing was correct. That is false. Every one of these pages already knows the moment its data arrived, and the Overview page has been reading exactly that since these bars were built. Nobody had ever asked it. I corrected the design brief that note was citing, because the brief is what the next person reads.

WHAT YOU WILL SEE

Open Invite codes, Bug reports, Users or Change requests. Same three things Overview has, same place, same behaviour. Bug reports is the one that matters most — it is an inbox, a row only appears when a customer somewhere hits Report a bug, and until now the only way to find out one had arrived was to leave the page and come back.

ONE THING I DELIBERATELY DID NOT DO

The card told me to write a note in the code explaining that the Crew page is permanently different. I did not, because you reversed that yourself the same day on another card — you asked whether Crew should just fold into the same refresh as everything else, and the answer there is yes. Writing a paragraph defending an exception on the day you have asked to remove it is a document that is stale before it is saved. Instead a test now goes red the moment Crew is folded in, so that night has to delete Crew's own "checked 2 minutes ago" line at the same time — otherwise the page would tell you how fresh it is twice.

HOW HARD I LOOKED

All eight staff pages, both light and dark, driven in a real browser: 106 readings, none wrong. Then the same run against the old code as a control: 20 failures, in exactly the shape described above. The toggle is clicked rather than just looked at, because a switch that draws two states and changes neither is the sort of thing that ships looking finished.

eyeItems.title: Your Usage pane, before and after — and the reason it said zero is not the reason anyone expected
eyeItems.question:
WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING AT. Two pairs and one single. First pair: the Usage pane on the live studio, then on tonight's build. Second pair: the Refer a friend footer, the same way. Last one: Profile, where Remove now works.

THE THING WORTH TWO MINUTES, and it is the diagnosis rather than the fix. You said Usage was showing you had used no credits. It was — and the sum was RIGHT. Your last paid roll was 30 August. The month rolled over on 1 September. The pane was adding up "this month", and this month, at the moment you looked, genuinely had nothing in it. Adding harder would have given you the same zero.

So there was nothing wrong with the arithmetic and two things wrong with the WINDOW. Your account has no billing period at all — it is a free plan, so there is no monthly cycle recorded against it — and the pane invented a calendar month to stand in for one. Worse, the "of 5,000 this month" it measured you against does not exist: a free account's credits are handed over once, at signup, and NOTHING ever tops them back up. That line was promising you a refill that never comes.

It now says what it actually knows. Where there is a real billing period it uses that period and its real allowance. Where there is not, it says "in the last 30 days" and tells you what you have left. Your figure moves when you cast, which is the thing you were telling us it did not do.

THE ONE I WENT LOOKING FOR AFTERWARDS IS WORSE THAN THE ONE YOU REPORTED. The same mistake — measuring against a cycle that does not run — was on the Billing pane twice, and one of them is embarrassing: the bar is capped at full but the sentence beside it is not, so on your own account (24,535 credits against a 5,000 "allowance") that pane has been reading "491% of this month's allowance left". Both are gone.

ALSO IN THESE FRAMES. "Frames made" is gone, and not because it was confusing — because it was false. It was counting charged operations, and on your account those are nineteen different things including "Mint package" and "Evidence package synchronization", neither of which makes a frame, while "Refresh views" makes several for one charge. You said not to keep a number nobody can name, so it went. The Refer a friend links were 16px against an 11px sentence and are 11px now. Bio is gone from Profile on your word — the field only; anything already written is still in your own data export. And Remove actually removes: I put a real picture on a test account, clicked it, and checked afterwards that the picture went back to the default AND the file left our storage rather than being left behind.

NOTHING HERE NEEDS A DECISION unless the last-30-days window is not what you want. If you would rather Usage showed all time, or the current calendar month with an honest label, say so and it is one line.

AFTER — "Usage in the last 30 days", 7,895 used, and the note says what is left instead of an allowance that never renews. Two tiles, not three.
BEFORE — "Redeem a code" and "Who has joined" at 16px, towering over the row they sit on.

eyeItems.title: Eyebrows the studio drew on a face that has none - and they measure bigger than real ones
eyeItems.question:
WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING AT - no question for you this time, just something worth seeing.

All four faces were asked the same thing by the same piece of the studio: "where are the eyebrows?" The pale overlay is exactly what it answered. Nothing was placed by hand and nothing was picked for effect.

RIGHT COLUMN - two ordinary faces that have eyebrows. The overlay is on their eyebrows. Correct, both times.

LEFT COLUMN - two creatures with no eyebrow hair at all. Instead of "there are none", the studio painted eyebrows onto the bare ridge above the eyes. On the top one it drew a full matching pair; on the bottom one it drew a single brow and nothing on the other side, which tells you it is not even being consistent with itself.

THE NUMBER UNDER EACH FACE is how much the studio thinks it found. Read the top row: the invented pair (6,714) is bigger than the woman's real eyebrows (3,878). The invented one wins. So we cannot separate real from invented by size - and that closes off the simplest fix anyone would reach for.

Why it matters in the product: this is the step that checks our own work after you ask for something to be taken off. When it wrongly says the thing is still there, we do not update the face's record - so the next edit paints it back on. You would get what you asked for once, then lose it.

This does NOT need a verdict from you. The decision it feeds is on the card below it, and my recommendation there has changed because of it.

frames.caption: LEFT - two creatures with no eyebrow hair: asked for "eyebrows", the studio painted them onto the bare ridge (the pale overlay is its own answer, painted back), 6,714 px and 4,001 px. RIGHT - two ordinary faces asked the same word in the same sitting: 3,878 px and 6,084 px, correctly on their real brows. The invented pair outscores a real pair. Same answer twice on every face, so it is settled rather than a wobble. A blank grey picture through the same code correctly answered "nothing there".

eyeItems.title: ANSWERED — you said top crop on both, and the Delete dialog now takes it (#198 closed)
eyeItems.question:
A small one, and the only reason it needs your eye is that the obvious fix would have moved faces.

WHAT WAS WRONG. Sign and Delete are the same dialog with different words. The instruction that sizes the portrait in that dialog had a typo-shaped mistake in it — it was written to point at the picture, and it pointed one level off, so for as long as it has existed it has applied to NOTHING. The Sign portrait was being sized by the browser's default and then simply cut off at the bottom by the frame around it. The Delete portrait, by an accident of where its grey-out lives, DID get the instruction. So the same face in the same dialog shell was being cropped two different ways depending on which button you pressed.

It has never looked broken, and that is exactly why it survived: our own renders are all the same shape, so cutting the bottom off and cropping properly happen to land in the same place.

WHY IT NEEDED YOU. Making the instruction work as written centres the crop — which slides the face about 27 pixels. That is a change to two dialogs you have already accepted, so the card for this was filed rather than fixed, months ago, waiting for someone to put frames in front of you.

WHAT I DID INSTEAD. Anchored the crop to the TOP, which is where the browser was already cutting. Then measured it rather than trusting my own eye: the Delete portrait is pixel-for-pixel identical, not one pixel of 57,620 changed. The Sign portrait is not quite byte-identical — the picture is scaled by a very slightly different route now — but there is no movement in it, and I proved that by ALSO building the version that does move and measuring both through the same instrument. That is the third panel.

⚠ AND THE THIRD PANEL IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH SEEING. Centred is exactly what your DELETE dialog does today. On a standard 1024x1536 render the Delete portrait shows source rows 128 to 1408 — it takes 128 pixels off the top and 128 off the bottom — while the Sign portrait shows rows 0 to 1280, dropping 256 off the bottom and nothing off the top. So panel three is not a mock-up of a bad idea; it is a photograph of the other half of your own product, and the gap between panel one and panel three is the bug.

THE QUESTION: the left and middle panels should look the same to you. Do they? And now that you can see both crops side by side — is TOP the one you want in both dialogs, or would you rather I brought Sign across to Delete's centred crop instead? Either is one line; I chose the one that changes nothing you have already approved.

frames.caption: Same candidate, three ways. LEFT is what the Sign dialog draws today. MIDDLE is what it draws after tonight. RIGHT is the version I did NOT ship — the centred crop — a simulation of that rule on this face, labelled on the frame so it is never mistaken for a shipped screen. But the mechanism in it is live: it is exactly what your Delete dialog does. Left and middle should be indistinguishable to you. Right should not be, and that gap is the bug.
For context rather than judgement: the actual Sign dialog after the change, in light. Nothing in it moved but the mechanism behind the picture.

eyeItems.title: ANSWERED — your two cuts are recorded, and the hard ban stays off (#185)
eyeItems.question:
Two things you sent an hour apart, both fixed and both worth your eye, because the test you set is whether these words would cast EIGHT different people of that type rather than reprint the one in the picture.

FRAME 1 is the goth. What the reader used to say about it: "A woman in her twenties, slight build, long straight platinum hair with blunt bangs, multiple facial piercings and forearm tattoos. Dark-fashion / gothic-alternative model type, styled with lace bodysuit, leather choker and spiked eye harness." What it says now: "Woman in her twenties, dark-fashion / cyber-goth model type. Pale skin, sculpted platinum hair, facial piercings and fine-line facial markings, script tattoos on both arms. Athletic build, dark structured fashion in lace, leather and spiked metal accents." Your two men still read the way you approved them.

FRAME 2 is a creature from your own reference folder. It used to be answered "I couldn't find a person in that picture." It now reads: "Reptilian humanoid being of adult presence, solid muscular build, dark pebbled scaled skin with bony ridged crests along the face. Bone-toned spinal ornamentation breaks the scales. Menacing creature-alien performance type." A picture with no BEING in it — an object, a place — is still refused, and I kept a control for that in the test run.

TWO THINGS I OWE YOU STRAIGHT.

One. I did NOT add a code ban on the words you struck (bodysuit, choker, harness, slight), and that was a judgement call I could be wrong about. The reason is that your own PASSING examples use those same kinds of words — "fitted dark crew-neck top" is a named garment and "athletic muscular build" is build language — so a ban wide enough to catch the bad use also refuses your good ones. It is the "shave"/"shape" problem this studio has hit three times. So the rule lives in the reader's instruction, and the proof lives in running it on real pictures rather than in a test that can only check itself. If you would rather have the hard ban and accept that it will sometimes refuse a good description, say so and it is one change.

Two. Across fourteen reads, none used any word on your drop list and every build word came from the short list of families. About one read in three still slips in a single named item — "a buckled choker", "a mechanical eye-piece". That is the honest remaining gap, not something I am claiming is finished.

THE QUESTION: do these two read as TYPES you could cast eight different people from, or is there still inventory in them?

pipeline.title: The file guarding who may look at a customer's account was checking almost nothing
pipeline.note:
This is the file that is supposed to prove only the right staff can open a customer's account, read their audit trail, or look at what they have been charged. It reported 46 checks. 42 of them could not fail.

Most were writing an answer down and then agreeing with it - one, under a heading reading 'Access Control', literally checked that the word "moderator" equals the word "moderator". Another said 'should not provide unblock capability' and then checked that true is true.

Two real holes were underneath. Nowhere in the whole codebase did anything check that an ADMIN can actually use the moderator screens - a promise the product makes in writing. And not one of the twelve 'read' actions on that screen was ever exercised: the audit log, the user list, the blocked addresses, the credit history a staff member opens when a customer complains about a charge. All twelve run for real now.

Every replacement was proved by deliberately breaking the product 33 different ways and checking that the right alarm - and only the right alarm - went off each time. That includes one deliberate non-break which must set nothing off, so a crash can never be mistaken for an alarm.

The reviewer then found the sharpest thing of the night: one old check I had left alone because it looked fine was asking whether a password hash could leak onto the moderator screen - against a test customer who had no password hash. So it would have stayed green through exactly the leak it was named after. Measured: with that gap, the leak was staged and not one of the 34 alarms went off. Fixed and re-proved. The lesson is worth more than the fix - a clean-up pass is blindest to the checks it decided not to touch.

pipeline.title: A safety net with 104 knots in it, fifty of which were tied to nothing
pipeline.note: The change-request road is how a moderator asks an admin to refund credits, suspend an account or block an address - real money and real accounts. The file that is supposed to check that road reported 104 checks. Fifty of them checked nothing at all: they wrote down an answer, then confirmed the answer they had just written. One whole block of sixteen would have stayed green if we deleted the code it claims to test. Every one of the 104 was read by hand, because two attempts to count them automatically gave two different wrong answers. Fifty are gone or rebuilt to actually run the product; 55 remain and every one of them touches real code. Nine deliberate breakages were then made to the product to prove the new checks go off - eight did. The ninth did not, and it was a check I had just written this evening: it looked like it was proving that a moderator cannot pretend to be someone else, and it was proving nothing. It is two checks now, and both of them fire.

pipeline.title: 1.33 GB of abandoned copies of Drape were sitting in your temp folder
pipeline.note: Every time the team runs its safety checks before a deploy, it makes a private throwaway copy of the whole project, checks the code in it, and deletes it. About one time in fifteen the delete quietly failed and the copy just stayed - each one a quarter of a gigabyte. Nobody noticed because nothing goes wrong when it happens; it only costs disk. Yesterday's count was 7.8 GB across 32 copies, they were swept by hand, and FOUR had come back within a day - which is how we knew the leak was still running rather than a one-off. Tonight the sweep took 1.33 GB across 48 directories, and the code that leaks them is repaired, so they stop coming back.

pipeline.title: The team can finally tidy up after itself - its scrap files were unable to expire
pipeline.note: Each shift writes small throwaway scripts to check something, and the rule is that they get deleted a week later. The rule read the file's 'last modified' date - and back in August something rewrote that date on 270 of them in a single hour, so every one of them looked brand new and nothing could ever be deleted. The pile has grown from 379 files to 856 while that was true. It now works out a file's real age from the job it was written for - the card it belongs to, and the date that card closed, which lives on GitHub where nothing on your machine can touch it. 128 files are now provably old enough to go. They have NOT been deleted yet, on purpose: the tool is a day old, and its first act should not be an irreversible deletion. The next check-up runs it again and deletes only what both readings agree on.

pipeline.title: A test could report a verdict on something it had never actually run
pipeline.note:
Some of our safety checks work by installing a small script that runs when code is committed or pushed, then proving it refuses bad work. On Windows those scripts run whatever their file permissions say. On the machine that runs the checks for real, one wrong permission makes the script silently ignored - and the test carries on and reports that everything is fine.

It has happened twice. The second time, a test reported what a particular safety script can and cannot do - the finding an entire design decision rested on - over a script that had never run.

There is now a check that finds this shape anywhere in the suite. It was proved by deliberately breaking both of the real places, and by blinding it, which is the failure that matters: a checker that finds nothing looks exactly like a codebase with nothing wrong.

pipeline.title: A rollback on a shift branch could quietly sweep up your unsaved work (#611)
pipeline.note:
THE THING THIS PROTECTS. You and the night shifts share one folder on your machine. There is already a guard that stops a shift saving its work onto its own branch while sitting in your folder - because when that happened, it swept up whatever you had open and unsaved at the time. It has happened more than once.

WHAT WAS OPEN. That guard only ever watched an ordinary save. Git simply does not run it when you UNDO a change, copy one across, or replay a batch of them. So the one thing it existed to prevent could still happen, by a different door.

AND UNDOING A CHANGE IS NOW A ROUTINE ACT. Since your app started going live the moment something merges, the way we prove a change can be rolled back is to undo it. That turned the one road the guard was blind to into a road we walk on purpose.

WHAT IS DIFFERENT NOW. Undo, copy-across, replay and merge are all refused the same way an ordinary save was, with a message that says which branch, why, and exactly what to type to get out of it. Nothing changes for you working on the main line - that was checked in both directions.

WHAT THE CHECKING TURNED UP, AND IT IS THE part worth reading. The card that asked for this recommended a particular way of doing it. I built it and it does not work: that kind of guard is allowed to object but not to actually stop anything. The card had also ruled OUT the approach that turned out to be right, on a reason that applied to a different job. Both are now written down as measurements anyone can re-run, rather than as opinions.

A first version worked and was thrown away on cost: it would have added about a seventh of a second to every single git action you take, all night, to cover one rare case. What shipped costs that on saves only, and nothing at all the rest of the time.

Your reviewer found six real things across two rounds, including two sentences in my own notes that were simply false - one claimed a bypass flag would skip this guard when it does not, and one promised a way out that errors on the commonest road. Both were found by writing the test rather than by re-reading the sentence. All six fixed.

pipeline.title: Eight tools asked "am I the one being run?" eight different ways (#668)
pipeline.note:
NOTHING YOU WOULD HAVE SEEN, AND THAT IS THE PROBLEM. Several of our internal tools are both a thing another tool uses and a thing a person runs directly, so each had to work out which was happening. Eight of them worked it out in four different hand-written ways.

THE WAY IT GOES WRONG IS SILENT. One of those eight files carries a warning, written by whoever last got it wrong: on Windows the comparison can simply never match, so the tool does nothing, reports no error, and finishes successfully. A check that checks nothing and says it passed.

WHAT IS DIFFERENT NOW. All eight ask the platform instead - one built-in answer, nothing to spell wrong. The comments that explained the old approach were corrected rather than left behind, because a note describing machinery that no longer exists is how the next person is misled.

AND THE REVIEWER CAUGHT THE SAME TRAP HIDING IN THE FIX. The new built-in only exists on recent versions; on an older one it is silently false in both directions, which is the identical do-nothing-and-say-it-passed failure arriving through a different door. The two tools your commit process runs now refuse loudly on an old version instead, and the version requirement is written down - after a first attempt at writing it down allowed the exact versions that lack it.
