pipeline.title: The number under your switches was written before the night's work, not after (#618)
pipeline.note:
WHAT YOU ASKED. Yesterday morning: "how many bugs has it done and worked on its still reading as 18 but its been working all night".

YOU WERE RIGHT, AND THE COUNTING WAS NEVER THE PROBLEM. It was WHEN it ran. The number under each switch on your panel was written once, at the START of a shift, and never again. So it always told you what a shift FOUND when it arrived - never what it CLOSED before it left. On the night you asked, ten bug cards closed and the panel still showed you the morning's figure.

WHAT IS DIFFERENT NOW. A shift refreshes those numbers as it finishes. Close three bug cards tonight and the panel is three lower by morning, without anybody typing anything.

THE PART THAT NEEDED CARE. Adding work to the end of a shift means adding a way for the end of a shift to go wrong - and if that step dies, the shift's row is left open and your page says a shift is still running when it is not. That has happened before. So the counting runs only AFTER the shift is safely marked finished, and it cannot take the finish down with it: if the count fails for any reason, it says why, your numbers stay as they were, and the shift closes normally.

The reviewer found two real things and both are fixed: a count that HUNG rather than failed would still have hung the close (there is a time limit on it now), and a 'stay quiet' setting that was offered and never actually used. It also caught that one sentence I wrote about the change was wider than the change - that is corrected in the file rather than left for somebody to trip on.

pipeline.title: A mistyped case name ran nothing and printed ALL PASS (#642)
pipeline.note:
WHAT THIS IS ABOUT. Four of our own tools took typed instructions and quietly ignored anything they did not recognise. The one that matters: the command that stops leftover dev servers on your machine. Typing --kil instead of --kill did not produce an error - the tool listed the servers, exited cleanly, and killed nothing. You would read that as "there was nothing to stop", not as "you typed it wrong".

AND THE REVIEWER CAUGHT SOMETHING WORSE, WHICH I HAD DESCRIBED BACKWARDS. Two of our test tools let you name a single case to re-run. If you misspelled the name, the tool ran ZERO cases - and then printed ALL PASS and exited successfully. So somebody checking a fix, who typos the name, reads ALL PASS having tested nothing at all, and files the fix as verified. I had written in the code that a typo ran EVERY case; the opposite was true, and the opposite is the dangerous direction. Both tools now refuse a name they do not know and tell you the names they do.

WHY IT MATTERS TO YOU. None of this is your app - it is the night shift's own tooling. But a tool that reports success over nothing is how a shift comes to tell you something is fixed when it is not, and that is the one thing these reports are for.

TWO THINGS ARE LEFT ON THIS CARD, both recorded rather than rushed. One command uses -h for help and our checker does not speak it, so converting it naively would break a working command. And --kill with an unusable value still exits quietly having done nothing - a different fault from this one, and it needs a decision about what it should say.

pipeline.title: The command that puts your app live would accept a typo and deploy anyway (#642)
pipeline.note:
WHAT THIS IS ABOUT. Deploying Drape is one typed command. It has a rehearsal mode - you add the word --dry and it does everything except actually put the code live. It is the safety net you use when you want to check a deploy will work without doing it.

WHAT WAS WRONG. The command looked for the exact word --dry and ignored every other word you gave it. So --dryrun, or --dry-run, or a mistyped --dr, meant a REAL DEPLOY. There was no error and no warning - it simply did not see the word, decided you had not asked for a rehearsal, and shipped.

AND IT HAD A SECOND SWITCH NOBODY HAD WRITTEN DOWN. The deploy command also refuses to run while you are working, so a shift cannot deploy underneath you - and there is an override for when the deploy IS the thing you are waiting for. That override existed, seven hundred lines away from the first one, and the command's own instructions listed only one of its two switches. Anybody reading the manual would not have known the second was there.

WHAT IS DIFFERENT NOW. All seven of these tools now stop on a word they do not recognise and tell you which words they do take. Try to deploy with a typo and you get: REFUSING: unknown argument --dryrun. Known: --dry, --anyway. The two switches are written in one place and the refusal message is printed from that same place, so the manual and the behaviour cannot drift apart again.

THE OTHER SIX. Same class, same fix: the tool that reads your replies, the one that reports where everything stands, the one that seeds test data, two housekeeping checkers, and a database backfill. That last one is worth naming: it only writes when you give it --apply, so a mistyped --aply used to mean a silent rehearsal - the harmless direction, but the same blindness.

PROVED RATHER THAN ASSERTED. Every one of the seven was run with a deliberate nonsense word and refused. The rehearsal mode was run for real and got all the way through the deploy command's own checks. And the automatic guard that watches for this class was deliberately broken on a file I had just fixed, to confirm it would notice - it named the file. Your Fable reviewer read the whole thing and found no defects.

NOTHING A CUSTOMER TOUCHES CHANGED. These are the crew's own tools. Nothing here spends money, writes to your database, or goes near billing or logins.

pipeline.title: A checker that had to ask "am I the thing being run?" was asking it the sloppiest way (#642)
pipeline.note:
A small one, and the interesting part is why it could not be done the obvious way.

Some of the crew's files are two things at once: a library other tools borrow from, and a command a person can run. Each carries a line asking am I the one that was run? - because borrowing from it must not set it off.

This particular file asked that question by comparing FILE NAMES, which is the loosest possible version of it. It also read the typed command the old blind way. Fixing the second broke the first: the safety guard that watches this class quite rightly forbids a file from reading the command line twice, once carefully and once carelessly - a second careless reader beside a careful one is exactly the half-finished fix it exists to catch.

So it is answered with the platform instead of another hand-written comparison: modern Node has a built-in way to ask this, and it needs no reading of the typed command at all. Checked in our actual setup first, both ways round, before it was used.

Proved with the real borrower rather than a stand-in: the tool that genuinely imports from this file was run, and it did not set the checker off.

I also counted the rest of that family and left it alone: EIGHT more files ask the same question, in four different hand-written spellings, and one of them has a comment written by whoever last got it wrong - on Windows the comparison never matches, so the checker prints nothing and exits cleanly. A checker that checks nothing and reports success. That is filed as its own card rather than swept into this one.

pipeline.title: A change merged with your Fable reviewer never having looked at it - and the tool told the shift the wrong reason (#566)
pipeline.note:
WHAT THIS IS ABOUT. Every change the team makes goes past two checks before it merges: the machine gate (types, tests, the maps) and your Fable reviewer, which reads the change the way a senior engineer would. The gate is ours. The reviewer is yours - it runs on your Claude subscription and it is the one that catches judgement mistakes a test cannot.

WHAT WENT WRONG. On 5 September a change merged without the reviewer ever having run on it. That is allowed when the reviewer is down - the standing rules say an ordinary change may merge on the gate alone - but nobody knew it had happened. The shift's own log said nothing. It was only found a day later by someone querying GitHub by hand.

AND THE TOOL SAID SOMETHING WORSE THAN NOTHING. When a change touches money or logins, the merge tool holds it and prints why. Until tonight it printed: "no reviewer verdict exists (the reviewer looked at it and declined - check for a stale skip-review label)". That sentence is a confident diagnosis of a decision nobody made. There was no label. The reviewer had not declined anything; it had never run. A shift reading that goes hunting for something that is not there.

HOW OFTEN. I measured it rather than guessing: over the last 100 reviewer runs, 50 things happened that should have started a review, and 49 of them did. One did not.

WHERE THE FAULT IS - AND IT IS NOT OURS. One case gave a clean answer. On another change, the same label was applied, produced nothing, was removed fourteen minutes later, re-applied, and produced a review two seconds after that. Same change, same commit, same settings, same label - one worked and one did not. Nothing on our side differed between them, so the miss is inside GitHub's own delivery of the event, which we cannot see from here. I have written that down as the finding rather than inventing a cause that sounds plausible.

WHAT IS DIFFERENT NOW. The team's merge tool tells two things apart that it used to call by one name: the reviewer LOOKED and decided this change did not need a full read (normal, and it stays silent), versus NOTHING RAN AT ALL. The second one is now printed on the line the tool writes as it merges, so it lands in the shift's log at the moment it happens. The remedy is named in that line too.

WHAT DELIBERATELY DID NOT CHANGE. A missing reviewer still does not BLOCK an ordinary change - the rules already say merge on the gate alone when the reviewer is down, and changing that is your call, not a bug fix. Money and login changes are held exactly as hard as before, whichever kind of absence it is.

YOUR REVIEWER FOUND THREE THINGS IN THIS VERY CHANGE, and they are worth mentioning because two of them were in the new sentences. One was a wrong number I had put in the message. The other was sharper: my new line said the change was "merging on the gate alone, for a non-money change" - and it turns out a money change that a shift has hand-reviewed reaches that same line, where both halves of that sentence would be false. So the message now states the fact and never the reason. That is the exact mistake this whole change exists to stop, caught inside the fix for it.

pipeline.title: Press Annual and the value line stayed on the monthly rate - the two numbers in one card did not add up (#661)
pipeline.note:
WHAT YOU WOULD HAVE SEEN. Open Change plan and press Annual. The Starter card showed "$22 / month, billed yearly" - and directly above it, "2,778 CREDITS PER $1".

Those two numbers do not add up, and anyone can check it on their own screen: 75,000 credits divided by $22 is about 3,400, not 2,778. The price was doing the annual discount and the rate was still dividing by the monthly $27. The compare table said the same two things four rows apart - $22 in one row, 2,778 in another.

Add credits had the milder half of it. Turning Annual on changed what you pay and left the value line quoting the monthly rate, so the line that exists to argue the annual saving was the one line that did not move when you took it.

WHAT IT SAYS NOW. Annual on, Starter: "3,347 credits per $1" over "$22 / month, billed yearly". And it reproduces from the money we actually charge - 75,000 credits a month is 900,000 over a year, over the $268.92 a year costs, is 3,347 exactly.

NOTHING ANYONE IS CHARGED CHANGED. Every price and every charge is what it was; this is the sentence beside them.

HOW IT WAS FIXED, AND WHY IT WON'T COME BACK. Not by adding a second calculation - by removing one. There were three separate copies of "work out the price at the chosen interval" scattered across the two panels, and copies drift apart, which is exactly what happened. There is one now, and both the price and the rate read it, so they move together or neither moves.

Seen in the running app at both toggle positions, on both panels, in both themes.

pipeline.title: The tool that counts leftover copies of the app on your machine was seeing double (#658)
pipeline.note:
Nothing a customer sees - this is the crew's own housekeeping tool, and it is the one your rule about leaving processes running on your machine is enforced with.

WHAT WAS WRONG. When the app runs in development it is not one program but a small chain of them, and two links in that chain are Windows command shells. The tool only ever looked at one kind of program, so the shells were invisible - and with the chain broken in the middle, one running copy of the app was counted as two. Last night it reported eleven where seven were actually running.

WHY IT MATTERS. A shift reading eleven cannot tell its own leftovers from a double count, so it either leaves something running on your machine or spends time chasing a process that never existed.

WHAT IT DOES NOW. It reads the whole picture, follows the chain through the shells, and reports one running copy as one. Proved on this machine rather than argued: with one copy running, the old tool printed two and the new one printed one, and ending the one it names ends everything.

pipeline.title: Add credits was arguing value in a unit nobody can read - it now matches Change plan (#403)
pipeline.note:
WHAT YOU WOULD HAVE SEEN. Open Change plan and each rung argues its value as "3,145 CREDITS PER $1". Open Add credits and the same fact was written the old way: "0.036 cents a credit, down from 0.041 cents" - the figure you yourself called unreadable, because at that size the plans only differ in the third decimal.

One fact, two units, two panels. Anyone who opened both in one sitting met it twice in two shapes.

WHAT IT SAYS NOW. "2,941 credits per $1, up from 2,778" - the same sentence Change plan makes, in the same unit.

AND ONE THING FOUND BY LOOKING. On a free account the new sentence first read "2,778 credits per $1, up from free", which is not a comparison anybody can make - free is not a rate. The old sentence had exactly the same flaw and nobody had noticed. On a free plan the panel now simply says what you get, with nothing dangling on the end.

The frames are in your gallery below.

pipeline.title: Twelve more scripts that can be pointed at your live database now refuse a mistyped word (#642)
pipeline.note:
Nothing a customer sees. These are the scripts the team runs by hand against the database - the ones that create a table, or read your switch panel - and they each take one word telling them WHICH database: your live one, or the development copy.

WHAT WAS WRONG. Last night eighteen of them were taught to stop and say so when they are handed a word they do not recognise. Twelve MORE had quietly written out their own copy of that same instruction long ago - so they never got the lesson, and nothing noticed, because the check written to watch for this only looked at scripts that were using the shared version. A check that watches the ones that signed up cannot see the ones that never did.

Two of those twelve are the scripts that built the switch panel on this page.

WHAT IT COST IN PRACTICE. Less than it sounds, and worth saying plainly: a script handed only a MISSPELT database name already stopped - it could not tell which world you meant, so it refused. What it did NOT catch was a good word with a bad one beside it. Type 'live database, and only pretend to do it' and it heard the first half, ignored the second, and did the thing for real.

WHAT IT IS NOW. All thirty read the same one instruction, and a second check watches the whole folder rather than only the scripts that opted in - so the thirty-first cannot slip through the same gap.

THE PART WORTH YOUR TIME. The reviewer found that the new watcher could still be walked around by writing the same mistake across two lines instead of one. That is now closed rather than written down as a known weakness, and the walk-around is kept as a test so it cannot come back.

pipeline.title: Eleven leftover copies of the dev server were running on your machine, some since 4 September (#561)
pipeline.note:
Something on your own computer, so it is here rather than only in the queue.

WHAT WAS THERE. Every time someone looks at the app locally it starts a small server. It is supposed to be stopped afterwards. Eleven of them were still running tonight - the oldest from 4 September, four days ago - and two of them were holding the two doors (ports 3000 and 3001) that the team needs to open the app at all.

A card was filed about three of them on 5 September and correctly did not kill them, because it could not tell whether one was under your hand at the time. Three days later there were eleven, and nothing was running but this shift. All cleared. Your machine now reports none.

THE PART WORTH YOUR TIME. The tool that counts them was over-reporting. Starting the app is really TWO small programs, one starting the other - and because a Windows command window sits between them, the counter could not see they were related and listed both. Eleven rows were seven servers. Proved rather than reasoned: stopping seven of them ended all eleven. Filed as its own card with the measurement.

Also cleared: two empty folders left behind by an earlier tidy-up that Windows had refused to finish.

pipeline.title: A safety check was reporting a verdict without ever running (#640)
pipeline.note:
Nothing here is anything a customer sees. It is the safety net the team's own work runs through before it reaches your app - so when it is wrong, it is wrong quietly, and it is wrong about whether everything else is safe.

WHAT WAS WRONG. Before a shift sends work anywhere, it runs a quick set of checks. One of them tests a guard that stops anybody publishing to your live site by accident. To test it, the check has to actually run that guard and see what it decides.

It was not running it. The small program it needed was not where it looked, so nothing started - and instead of saying 'I could not run this', the check reported a number, and the test read that number as the guard's decision. Every shift saw a red mark it had not caused, on every piece of work. A red you always see is a red you stop reading.

THE PART THAT IS WORSE THAN THE CARD SAID. The same test came out GREEN or RED depending only on which window it was started from - same code, same minute. Two shifts could have told you opposite things and both been honest.

WHAT IT IS NOW. If the thing cannot be started, it says so and names what is missing, instead of inventing an answer. Seven other checks were moved onto the same rule.

THE PART WORTH YOUR TIME. This same fault had to be hunted three times, because each hunt searched for how it was WRITTEN rather than what it DID - and the last one found was the dangerous kind: a test that would have reported 'the safety guard blocked this' about a guard that never ran. So instead of hunting a fourth time, the list is now pinned: any new check of this shape has to be declared on purpose, and two that are still imperfect are named rather than quietly left out.

pipeline.title: Eighteen tools that write to your database stopped ignoring a mistyped word (#642)
pipeline.note:
Also invisible to customers, and this one is about your data.

WHAT WAS WRONG. Eighteen internal tools apply changes to a database - and half of them can be pointed at the LIVE one. Each is told which database to use, plus whatever else the operator meant. They read the database name and threw every other word away without saying anything.

A WORKED EXAMPLE. Somebody types the live database plus a second word to make the run a rehearsal. The tool reads 'live', never notices the second word, and does it for real.

WHAT WAS NOT AT RISK, because it matters that this is not overstated: mistyping the DATABASE name was always safe - no database was named, so the tool stopped. The danger was a mistyped word sitting next to a correct one.

MEASURED BOTH WAYS. All eighteen were run with a deliberately wrong extra word. Before: 18 out of 18 ignored it and carried on. After: 18 out of 18 stop and name it. One change, in one shared place, covering all eighteen.

WHAT IS LEFT. Twelve more tools of the same family were found that do not use that shared place at all - including the two that built your background-work switch panel. They are now written down by name as the next piece of work, rather than sitting inside a count.

pipeline.title: Eleven internal tools stop silently ignoring a word you typed wrong (#345)
pipeline.note:
None of this is anything a customer sees - it is the tools the team runs against your data and your app. But it is the kind of quiet fault that eventually costs you a wrong answer, so it is worth two minutes.

WHAT WAS WRONG. Eleven of these tools read the words you type after the command by looking only for the ones they expect. Anything else was thrown away without a word. So typing `--sinse` instead of `--since` did not produce an error - it produced a confident report about the last seven days, with the date actually typed nowhere in it. The same shape has already cost this project three times, once on the live site.

All eleven now refuse a word they do not know and print the words they do know. That is the whole change.

THE PART THAT WAS NOT EXPECTED. One of the eleven was on the list as harmless - it only reads and reports. It does not: run with one particular word and it clicks Follow in the real app, which spends credits. The check that is supposed to find every tool that can spend money could not see it, because that check looks at which billing code a tool imports, and this one spends by driving the app through a browser instead. It is now found by what it does rather than by what it imports, so the next tool that spends this way is covered without anyone remembering.

AND ONE REAL BUG FELL OUT OF IT. A tool that compares the codebase at two points in time took its two dates positionally. Put the optional setting first and it read the setting's name as one of the dates - and then reported a comparison of nothing at all, with no error. That is fixed, and the test checks it produces the right dates rather than merely that it does not crash.

The class is not finished and the card says so rather than closing quietly: 51 tools still read words this way, 18 of them through a single shared piece of code - so one fix covers eighteen. That is #642.

pipeline.title: The number telling you what nobody has looked at was resetting itself (#516)
pipeline.note:
Every night this page tells you how many jobs have gone a week with nobody looking at them. On 3 September that said NINE. The next night it said ZERO - and nobody had read a single one of those nine.

WHAT HAPPENED. The count asked GitHub 'when was this last touched?', and GitHub moves that date when ANYTHING changes on a job, including a label. The night before, a tidy-up had put labels on all nine at once. So the clock reset on the whole set, and the page told you the backlog had cleared itself.

That is the worst direction for a number like this to be wrong in: it hides work, and nothing looks broken while it does.

It now reads the job's actual history and counts only somebody commenting, closing, reopening, or a piece of work referencing it. Labels and filing do not count.

THE HONEST NEW NUMBER IS 14, NOT 1. And it disagrees with the old one in both directions, which is how I know it is measuring something real rather than just measuring differently. One job the old count called fresh had nothing on it but two labels - eleven days quiet. And the single job last night's report called rotten had actual work referencing it two days earlier - it was never rotten at all.

The sentence changed with it. It no longer says 'untouched', because that word is a claim nothing can support; it says what was actually measured, so a label can never make it false again.

The review found two faults in my first version and a third in my second, all taken. The sharpest: my own fix for the second one did not work. I had put a guard on a setting that limited how much of the queue got read - but tested against the real queue, that setting neither refused nor limited, because of how the data arrives in pages. A setting named 'limit' that does not limit is worse than not having it, so it is gone rather than guarded. There was never a sensible answer to 'how much of the queue should this number be about?' other than all of it.

pipeline.title: The warning badge on your own account: what the -11,600 actually is (#462)
pipeline.note:
Your account menu has a Moderation badge. It reads 1, and the one account it is counting is YOURS - flagged by the reconciliation scan at minus 11,600 credits. Nothing is at risk: that scan has been list-only since February and freezes nobody. But a warning light whose only warning is a false one is a warning light you stop looking at, so tonight was spent finding out what the number is.

THE GOOD NEWS FIRST, because it is the bigger half. Split the account in two - everything charged the modern way (a roll, a refine, a sign) against everything from the old studio - and the modern side balances EXACTLY: 58,740 credits taken, 58,740 credits accounted for. The other account with modern charges balances exactly too. So every roll you do today lands on the clean side, and this number does not grow.

The whole gap is one old thing. Back in late July the parked evidence composer wrote 45 records worth 11,450 credits. The jobs that did that work charged 9,300 and were separately refunded - but those 45 records never noted which job they belonged to, so the scan counts the same work twice: once through the job that charged for it, and again through the records left loose. Take those 45 out and your account reads minus 150 instead of minus 11,600.

The card was filed on a different theory - that FAILED pictures were being counted but never charged - and that turned out to be wrong, which is worth saying because the wrong theory is the cheaper mistake to make twice.

The fix itself is deliberately NOT done here. Correcting a money-adjacent instrument on a night shift's judgement is exactly what the rules say not to do, and there are three sensible ways to do it. It is card #638 with the three roads and a recommendation. What landed tonight is the diagnosis, written into the code where the wrong explanation used to be, and four tests that hold today's wrong answer in place so whoever fixes it has to say what they are changing.

One thing worth knowing about how we work: the note in that file used to say the number was PLUS 1,050 and explained why. It had been there twelve days, nothing had re-checked it, and it is not what the rows say. My first draft called that a mistake - the automatic reviewer caught me over-claiming, because that figure had actually been measured twice on the day. So the file now says what is true (the old reading recorded a conclusion and none of its workings, so nobody can tell) instead of what was tidier.

pipeline.title: The Sign button's aim, when you keep two faces in the same two seconds (#576)
pipeline.note:
A small one, and nothing you can hit changes. When you keep a face, the dock's Sign button points at the last one you kept. The code's own note said so. It is true if you keep one face - and not quite true if you keep two inside the same couple of seconds, because in that window they arrive in the order they sit on the SHEET rather than the order you clicked. Keep 08 then 03, and the button aims at 08.

It is left working exactly as it does, on purpose: fixing it properly means changing something every part of the keep machinery reads, which is a lot of risk for a two-click window - and nothing can be signed by accident anyway, because the confirm step shows you her face, her name and the price before any credits move.

What changed is that the sentence now has tests standing behind it, so the note and the behaviour cannot quietly drift apart again - which is the only thing the card was actually complaining about. The reviewer then found the same retired sentence sitting in the NEXT file along, which our own sweep had missed; that is corrected and held by a test too.

pipeline.title: Your spend 'this cycle' was counting money from the cycle before (#624)
pipeline.note:
You said "(a), fix it, not urgent" - this is (a), built and live.

A billing period starts at the moment somebody pays, so it starts in the middle of a day. We were adding up spend in whole DAYS, from the start of whichever day the period began on - so everything a customer spent that morning, before their renewal, was being counted as this cycle's. Worked example: renewal at 2pm, 9,000 credits spent that morning and 1,000 after it. Change plan said 10,000 spent. It should say 1,000.

That matters more than it sounds, because on day one or two of a cycle that figure is divided by a very small number of days to work out how fast somebody is burning credits - and THAT is what decides which plan the one highlighted button offers them. A wrong number there sells the wrong plan.

The studio now asks the ledger the question directly - what has this account spent since the exact minute their period began - instead of reassembling it out of a daily chart. Two other things fall out of the same change: a 90-day limit that meant an annual subscriber's spend could never be added up properly is gone, and the Usage pane and the two money windows now quote ONE figure instead of each working it out separately.

Proved on a real database, not just in theory: the 9,000 and the 1,000 above are actual rows, and the old method is run against the same rows in the same test so the two answers are shown to differ rather than claimed to.

pipeline.title: Your Free plan line no longer makes a promise a price change could break (#621)
pipeline.note: You chose (b), the safer line. Six of your seven lines say who a plan is FOR. The Free one also promised "a few casts a month, no card" - both true today, and both something a pricing decision could quietly turn into a lie, on the screen where people pay you. It now reads "For trying the studio out before you commit." Nothing is lost: the line directly underneath still says 5,000 a month, about 14 casting frames. Frames are in your gallery.

pipeline.title: A mistyped spending limit could switch the limit OFF instead of setting it (#625)
pipeline.note: This is house money, not yours, and nothing has been overspent. Our own measuring scripts take a spending ceiling on the command line - and if somebody typed the letter O instead of a zero, the ceiling did not become wrong, it stopped existing: every check against it silently passed. Five scripts read numbers that way. They now share one reader that refuses a value that is not a number, and any future script joins that protection automatically rather than by somebody remembering.

pipeline.title: Pictures put here for you could vanish off this page before you had looked (#354)
pipeline.note: Nearly happened last night. This gallery only shows items marked "open", and a nightly tidy-up marked them finished as soon as the underlying job closed - so two pictures uploaded for your eyes would have appeared nowhere at all, on the very edition asking you to look at something. A job finishing means the WORK is done; it does not mean you looked. Pictures now stay until somebody says you have seen them.

pipeline.title: The tool that lands the team's work could not do the one job it was built for (#630)
pipeline.note: You asked in September for the nights to stop idling while they wait. Part of that answer was a tool that tidies up when two jobs collide - and tonight it sat repeating "waiting" every thirty seconds, for over an hour, while holding the very action that would have unblocked it. It has been that way since it was built, because every test of it was run against the one situation where the fault cannot show. Fixed, and proved by watching it unblock and land the job it had been stuck on.

pipeline.title: The last two money-spending scripts now refuse a word they do not recognise (#602)
pipeline.note:
Housekeeping on the team's own tools, and it closes a job left half done in August.

The scripts that spend our money on test renders used to read their instructions by looking only for the words they expected, and quietly throwing away anything else. So a typo went unnoticed and the script did the expensive thing on its defaults. Twelve were repaired; two were left out for a stated reason - their published instructions use a slightly different style of wording that the checker did not understand, and rewriting the instructions people follow is a different decision from tightening a checker. The checker understands both styles now, so nothing anybody types has changed and both scripts are covered.

The reviewer then found a related hole in the same script, older than any of this: the spending CEILING is a number, and typing it with a letter O instead of a zero made it not-a-number - which does not raise the ceiling, it removes it entirely, because every comparison against not-a-number quietly answers no. A run could have gone ahead with no spending limit at all. It refuses by name now, proven both ways at the keyboard. Four more places with the same shape are written down as their own job rather than swept in beside this one.

pipeline.title: The automatic reviewer caught the fix carrying the same fault, one step further out
pipeline.note:
Worth telling you, because it is the review paying for itself and because it is the same story twice.

The repair adds your spend up over a window - and the report it adds from only ever goes back 90 days. On a MONTHLY plan that is fine, since a month sits well inside 90 days. On an ANNUAL plan it is not: the sum covered three months while the division still used the ten or eleven months the year had run. Traced on the reviewer's own example - somebody 200 days into an annual year spending a steady 1,000 credits a day - the panel would have said 450 a day, put the run-out date two months late, and recommended a plan BELOW what they actually use.

So the first fix would have oversold monthly customers and undersold annual ones. That is the identical mistake pointing the opposite way: a figure and a stretch of days that do not describe the same thing.

It is closed by making it impossible rather than by correcting the arithmetic - the spend and the number of days it covers now travel together, so no piece of code can be handed one without the other. Six deliberate acts of sabotage were run to prove every test involved can actually go red.

One related thing is written down and NOT fixed, because it needs a change on the server rather than on the screen: a billing period starts at a time of day and the usage report only speaks in whole days, so the first day of a cycle can carry a few hours of the previous one. Small, bounded, and filed as its own job.

pipeline.title: Change plan was about to sell the wrong plan to your first paying customer (#385)
pipeline.note:
When somebody opens Change plan or Add credits, the top of the panel tells them how fast they are spending and when they will run out: "At this rate you run out on the 9th... Studio covers the way you are actually working." Every one of those numbers was built by taking the credits an account has spent IN ITS ENTIRE LIFE and dividing that by the days elapsed in ONE month.

That is not just a wrong sentence. The same number decides which plan gets the one dark Upgrade button. Put in front of the real app on a test account - ten days into a month, 40,640 credits spent this month, 120,000 spent ever - the panel said Studio at $159 a month. The truthful reading says Pro at $68. It was recommending a plan $91 a month dearer than the customer needs, on the strength of a claim about their own usage that was not true.

Nobody has ever seen either number, and that is luck rather than design: the panel only draws once an account has a real billing period, and no account has one yet. It goes live silently the day somebody subscribes.

The fix adds the spend up from the ledger over the actual billing period - the same repair the Usage pane got in August after you spotted 115,695 used sitting next to of 5,000 this month. Both screens read one shared piece of code now, so they cannot drift apart and quote you two different figures for the same month.

One more thing was corrected on the way past: the small label above that figure said THIS MONTH over a number covering a billing period, which for most subscriptions is not a month. It says THIS BILLING PERIOD.

pipeline.title: The dock says which kept face Sign will act on (#556)
pipeline.note:
YOUR WORDS, on the 5th, with two frames: "if i select multiple casts to keep somehow i can sign all of them at once? this makes no sense?"

You were reading it exactly right. With four faces kept, the dock said "4 kept" and the button beside it said "Sign to roster" - and nothing anywhere said WHICH of the four it meant. It has only ever signed one: the highlighted face in the strip. The interface simply never told you that.

It now reads "4 kept - 05 selected", the chosen face is ringed more strongly, and the other three step back a little while a choice is live. Nothing about the money or the ceremony changed - the same one face, the same 450 credits, the same confirmation showing her picture before anything is spent.

TWO THINGS THE CARD ASKED FOR WERE REFUSED, and both were your own earlier rulings. The card wanted the button to read "Sign 08 to roster - 450 credits". You ruled on 2 August that the button names no face because the ring already says who, and D-109 says a price never sits in button text. Both are guarded by tests, so the fix went where it belonged - into the sentence - rather than through two of your decisions.

The review then found something the fix had missed: with FIVE kept the strip only draws four, and the one it was aiming at was the hidden fifth. So the sentence named a face you could not see. Fixed and re-photographed at exactly that state, and the label now names the roll too when your kept faces span more than one - because "03" means a position within a roll, and on a twice-rolled sheet it names two different people.

ONE THING WAS CHANGED FROM WHAT THE CARD ASKED, and it matters because it is about money. The card said the tag should appear on every failed tile without exception. There is one kind of failure that was never charged in the first place - its own line reads "Didn't start - not charged". That tile wears no refund tag, and a test now holds every kind of failure to the sentence a customer actually reads, so the two can never drift apart.

Every card that is on your desk today keeps exactly the meaning it has now.

pipeline.title: The crew's pre-flight check stopped failing for no reason (#548)
pipeline.note:
Housekeeping on the team's own tools, and it is the kind that quietly costs you nights.

Before a shift sends any work for checking, it runs a quick check of its own on this machine - about three minutes, to catch the obvious things before the slow seven-minute check does. That quick check had started failing at random: a handful of the crew's tests start real background programs, and when the whole set runs at once those programs occasionally take a second or two longer than the five seconds they were allowed. A DIFFERENT few failed each time, which is the giveaway - nothing was broken, they were just being crowded out.

That matters more than it sounds. A check that cries wolf is a check the next shift starts skipping, and then the slow expensive one goes back to catching everything. Measured before touching anything: on a full run of 12,495 tests, five failed for this reason alone. After: zero, out of 12,505 - and every one of them now finishes SLOWER than when it was failing, which is the proof it was the stopwatch and not the work.

The fix gives those tests thirty seconds instead of five, and - this is the part worth the words - it works out for itself WHICH tests need it, by reading the code, rather than keeping a list. A list would stop being right the first time somebody adds a test, which is how this sort of thing comes back.

THE AUTOMATIC REVIEWER EARNED ITS KEEP TWICE HERE. It found that the code doing that working-out had a blind spot which could make it overlook a test entirely and report all clear. Chased down, that was not a theory: one real test file was already invisible to it. Fixed, and the reviewer then re-did the whole calculation independently, by hand, and got exactly the same twenty-one files - which is better evidence than anything I could offer for it myself.

One thing found on the way and NOT fixed here, because it is a different fault wearing the same coat: another single test fails about one run in three for an unrelated reason. It is written up on its own with the evidence, and it needs a small decision about what that test should promise rather than a number changed.

pipeline.title: Five signposts pointed at safety nets that do not exist (#647)
pipeline.note:
Small, and it goes to something this project has been burned by twice.

All through the code there are notes saying, in effect, 'the test that guards this is over there'. Five of them named a file that is not in the project. Nothing was broken by that - but somebody who follows one of those signposts, finds nothing, and concludes the safety net was never built has just written off a net that is actually there. That exact mistake has twice cost this project months.

THE ONE THAT MATTERED MOST, AND THE ANSWER IS GOOD NEWS. Two of the five sat on the code that keeps your customers' casting recipes - their words and their pictures - out of the logs. Nobody knew whether the guard existed under another name or had never been written. It exists, twice, and both were read at the actual test before anything was changed. The protection has been working the whole time; only the signpost was wrong.

A check now reads every one of these signposts across the whole project and refuses any that names nothing. Where a note deliberately mentions a test that was DELETED - explaining what was removed and why - that is allowed and written down with the reason, because a note explaining that something died is worthless if it cannot name what died.

The job the card described was slightly wrong in two places and both were corrected against the code rather than followed: it counted six faults where there are five (the sixth is one of those deliberate mentions), and it asked for three exclusions that turned out not to be needed. The reviewer then caught me making the same class of mistake myself - a comment of mine explaining the exclusions was simply untrue about the project. That is corrected too, and the check now reads a quarter more of the project than it did.

pipeline.title: The crew's pre-flight check stopped failing at random for the second reason (#652)
pipeline.note:
Nothing a customer sees. This is the quick check every shift runs before it sends work anywhere - and last night's fix removed one reason it went red for no cause. There was a second.

WHAT WAS WRONG. When the check runs, it makes a throwaway copy of the app in a temporary folder, tests against it, then clears it away. It then asked: is that folder gone? On Windows the answer is often no - the system refuses to delete a folder something is still holding, even after the copy has been properly cancelled. So about one run in three, a shift saw a red mark caused by nothing it had done.

WHY THAT MATTERS MORE THAN IT SOUNDS. A check that goes red at random is a check people stop reading. It went red twice on a shift last night, on work that had nothing to do with it.

WHAT IT ASKS NOW. The real question was never 'is the folder gone' - it was 'has the copy been properly cancelled', because a copy left registered breaks the NEXT run. Those two turned out to come apart: driven 120 times under load, 8 folders were left behind and ZERO copies stayed registered. So the check now asks the question it actually cares about, and that one has a reliable answer.

WHAT IT FOUND ON THE WAY. Those leftover folders were real and they had been piling up - 7.8 GB of them on your machine, 32 complete copies of the app at about 275 MB each. Cleared tonight. The code that makes them is unchanged, so they will come back; that is now its own card with the measurement in it, rather than a test failing about it forever.

pipeline.title: The cards you have answered that still need you are now watched everywhere an open one is (#649)

THE FIRST. There is an automatic sweep that catches a card you have answered which your page still shows as needing you - it exists because that once went unnoticed for three days. It could not see the new answered-but-still-yours cards at all, because the piece of it that reads them was in a folder the checker never looked in. It looks there now, and it proves it looked: if that folder ever falls out of range again, the check goes red instead of quietly passing.

THE SECOND, and this one is a limit rather than a fix. There is one gap left: if you reply a SECOND time on a card that is already in the answered-but-still-yours state, nothing watches that reply. The clean repair needs your page to record WHEN a card's state last changed, and it does not record that today - so rather than bolt on something that would flag every card wrongly, the gap is written down at the exact line, and a check now makes sure that written note cannot outlive the code it describes. Closing it properly is its own small card.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN AND IS YOURS. The chip that says 'answered - still yours to do' appears on cards and not on picture sets in your gallery. Whether it belongs there is something to look at rather than reason about, so it was left alone for your eye.

problems.title: A paying customer is sent to a web address we do not run, the second their payment goes through
problems.detail: Found by the automatic code review on tonight's change, then checked against the live service. When somebody finishes paying, Stripe sends them back to https://drape.app — and our production site is not drape.app. It is a THIRD name: not drape.ai (the old one you are retiring) and not klieglabs.com (the live one). It appears nowhere else in the product as a real address. The same name is used for the 'manage my subscription' return. NOT FIXED tonight, deliberately: this is the money path, and two things need settling first — whether drape.app resolves to anything at all, and whether any real checkout has ever hit it. Card #467 has both, and says plainly not to fix it from reasoning alone.

problems.title: Your Billing pane has been telling you "491% of this month's allowance left" - found by sweeping for the fault you reported
problems.detail:
You reported one wrong number. The rule here is that a bug found once is a pattern until proven otherwise, so I went looking for the same mistake elsewhere - a figure measured against a monthly cycle the product does not actually run.

It was on the Billing pane twice, and the second one is worse than the one you reported. The little bar under CREDITS REMAINING is capped at full, but the sentence beside it is not - so with 24,535 credits against a nominal 5,000 "allowance", your own Billing pane reads "491% of this month's allowance left". The plan card had the same shape: "5,000 credits/mo" for credits you are given once.

Both are gone. Where you have a real subscription with a real renewal date, both lines come back and are true. Nothing changed for a paying account.

problems.title: The Usage zero you reported is fixed - and the number was never wrong, the window was
problems.detail:
Your words: "its also showing that i've used no credits".

Read against your real spend rows before anything was changed: your last paid roll was 30 August, the month rolled over on 1 September, and the pane was summing "this month". The zero was arithmetically correct and completely useless.

Two real faults sat underneath it. Your account has no billing period, so the pane invented a calendar month to measure against; and the "5,000 this month" it compared you to does not renew at all - a free account is given its credits once and nothing ever tops them up. The pane now uses your real billing period where there is one, and "the last 30 days" where there is not, with what you have left instead of a fictional allowance.

Fixed and deployed with this edition. Frames are on your desk below.

problems.title: Your nights were being counted as idle when they were not — a shift that worked was helping to stop the team
problems.detail: Your nights stop themselves after three shifts in a row report that there was nothing to do. That is the mechanism you asked for, so the team stops spending money to conclude nothing. It was reading the reports wrongly. A shift last night was titled "NOT a quiet night" and opened "This shift had work"; it had closed one card and filed another. The check looked for the words "quiet night" anywhere near the top and found them — inside the denial. So a working shift was counted as an idle one, and the note telling you three shifts had been quiet named a report whose own headline said the opposite. Fixed tonight: a shift now has to DECLARE it, not merely mention it. Quoting the phrase, denying it, or writing about the mechanism cannot trip it any more. Checked against all 155 shift reports ever written: eleven change verdict, and three of those were this exact mistake — including a second one from Sunday that nobody had spotted. It fails in the safe direction: if a genuinely quiet shift forgets to declare itself, the team keeps working rather than stopping.

problems.title: Your desk asked you to run a command you had already run — corrected tonight, and it is the second time
problems.detail:
Filed and closed as #344 on 2 September; nothing is outstanding on your page.

— resolved 2 September (#439). The original reading is kept below so the history stays readable.

The card about naming your queue's cards sat at the top of your desk telling you to run a database command. You ran it on Monday morning, 31 August. The work was merged, deployed and working the whole time the card was asking for it. Nothing was broken and nothing was at risk here — the cost is your attention, which is the scarce thing. What makes it worth a line rather than a quiet fix is that it is the same shape as the near miss on 31 August, where a card's recommendation told you to delete three Casts four hours after its own notes recorded that two of them were ones you wanted kept. Both cards were correct in their bodies and stale in the one sentence you actually read. The four automatic checks on your page all ask whether a card's STATE is out of date; none asks whether its ADVICE is. That gap is written up as #344 and the weekly review picks it up next.

problems.title: Fixed — the Invite label is the same size as Home and Casting now
problems.detail: You reported it at 21:57 last night; it is merged and on your rail. It was rendering at 16px — the page's ordinary text size — against 9.5px for every destination above it. Now 9.5px, measured in the browser rather than read off the stylesheet, in both themes and on the casting page too. Your fix was right and your diagnosis was one step off, which is the only part worth your attention: the nav labels were ALREADY 9.5px, so Invite was not one step too big — it sits outside the nav item that carries the size and was inheriting the page instead. That is why the size went on the label's own class rather than on the Invite rule: the next label put outside a nav item cannot repeat it. Frames below.

problems.title: Your nights stopped for about two hours last night and nothing told anyone — you found it yourself
problems.detail: Between 11:25 and 11:45 yesterday morning, four shifts launched and died in the same second they started. Each one exited with a success code and an empty log, so the runner counted every one as a good shift, waited ten minutes, and launched another into the same wall. Four of your own ordered cards sat untouched. You spotted it by noticing two close-stamps ten minutes apart; no instrument would ever have told you. The cause was found and fixed by the relay: the standing orders had grown past the length Windows allows on a command line, so the shift was never actually starting. That is repaired — the orders are handed over on a different channel with no limit at all. What landed tonight is the part that stops it being SILENT next time, which is the half that matters. Three things now hold. If the standing orders are ever unreadable, missing, truncated or absurdly long, the nights refuse to start and say so with the number, instead of launching into nothing. If two shifts in a row produce nothing at all, the nights stop themselves and leave you a note, then restart on their own the moment anything real happens. And when a launch fails outright, the reason is written down beside the empty log rather than lost with it. One more was found while sweeping for others like it, and it was worse than the original: if the small gatekeeper that decides whether to start a shift had ever gone missing or broken, the nights would have gone quiet FOREVER — no shifts, no notes, no stamps, nothing to notice at all. That is fixed too. There is no pull request for any of this and that is not an omission: these files run the night shifts and deliberately sit outside the codebase, so no automatic test can ever see them. In their place there is a script that drives the real runner against a sandbox — 36 checks, and it includes a deliberate sabotage proving the checks would actually fail if the guard stopped working.

problems.title: Your Cast still will not delete — and the reason we had written down was the wrong one
problems.detail:
Fixed on 31 August (#308) — the Cast deleted, and the same fault was quietly blocking two others.

— resolved 2 September (#439). The original reading is kept below so the history stays readable.

This is the thing you asked about, and it is not fixed. What IS fixed tonight is a different fault that we had blamed on the same line.

Your Cast "yejjjee" has nine accepted-candidate pictures attached. Before the deletion will let go of a picture it checks the picture's filename against a pattern. Those nine are filed under a folder called "candidates"; the check insists they be under "plates". They are yours, they belong to that Cast, and the studio itself filed them that way. Twenty-seven other Casts deleted cleanly the same morning — yours is the first you have tried that has one of these pictures.

I did not fix it because two different parts of the studio file the same kind of picture under two different folder names, so no single answer is right for both — and this is the code that deletes permanently. Getting it wrong means either deleting pictures that should have been kept or keeping ones that should have gone. That is a judgement on a destructive path, so it waits for the Fable seat and your allowance.

One consequence worth having in front of you: Library is the only door left for removing a legacy Cast, so it must NOT be stubbed out before this lands, or your three old Casts are stranded. Written up with the measurements as #308.

problems.title: A tidying-up check has been reading two different things as one for months, and nobody could have seen it
problems.detail:
Carded as #274 and sitting under your Housekeeping switch. It is maintenance, not a problem.

— resolved 2 September (#439). The original reading is kept below so the history stays readable.

Not urgent and nothing is broken for a customer. It is worth two minutes because of what it means rather than what it costs.

We have a check that stops anyone deleting code without a written decision about it. Removing the word "Klieg" from the top bar tonight made that check go red — and the thing it named was not the thing I had changed. There are TWO pieces of code called BRAND_NAME: the one in the new interface, and an old one buried in the legacy casting engine that nothing has used for a very long time. The check looks them up by NAME ONLY, so for as long as the new one was in use it was vouching for the old one as well.

So the honest summary is: a check we rely on to tell us what is dead can report "all clear" for something nobody has touched in months, purely because something else shares its name. Nothing was deleted; both are written down with reasons. Fixing the check properly means re-taking every reading it has ever produced, which is a night of its own — filed as #274 rather than half-done tonight.

problems.title: Your Fable allowance is still out - about five days now, and tonight's red tick was NOT one of them
problems.detail:
The reviewer is back and #219 closed on your word. Proven rather than assumed: it ran on both of tonight's changes and returned full written verdicts, one of which found a real miss of mine.

— resolved 2 September (#439). The original reading is kept below so the history stays readable.

Still down. Every pull request since has merged on the machine gate alone, which your standing rule allows for a change that touches no money and no login path.

TONIGHT IS DIFFERENT AND WORTH ONE PARAGRAPH, because the page would otherwise show you another red tick and you would reasonably read it as another refusal. Tonight's change edits the reviewer's own settings file. The reviewer refuses to run on any change to its own settings - that is a deliberate safety rule on their side, not ours - so our gate deliberately turns the tick RED rather than letting it go green over a review that never happened. I read the action log rather than the tick, and it says in its own words: "NO VERDICT - the reviewer cannot run on its own change". The change was reviewed by hand instead and that review is written on the pull request, which is what that rule asks for.

The thing that is easy to get backwards, and it is why the log gets read every time: a RED review tick does NOT mean the reviewer rejected the change. It means NO REVIEW WAS PRODUCED. A real verdict rides a GREEN tick, as a comment.

Opus is answering fine on the same machine and the same login - it ran tonight's whole shift. It is your Fable 5 allowance specifically, and N1 stays open until it can do the milestone read.

problems.title: Last night's briefing was written and never reached your page - and the fact you are reading this is the proof it is fixed
problems.detail: Edition 93 was finished and pushed at 10:07 yesterday morning and you never saw it. Railway built the new version perfectly - the build log is clean and the finished image was uploaded at 00:13 - and then the container that was meant to run it never started. It produced not one line of output for twenty-nine minutes and was stopped. The deploy ceremony watched for thirty minutes, refused to report a deploy it had not seen finish, and exited with an error, which is exactly what it is for. It was not our change: the only difference between that version and the one that was running is eleven lines of the briefing file itself. Your studio was never affected - production stayed healthy on the previous build the whole time, no credits, no renders, nothing a customer could touch. The one cost was that a night's journal sat where you could not read it, and the single thing needing your answer was already on the page you could see. Tonight's push carries both editions' news. If this ever happens twice in a row it stops being a stall and becomes an infrastructure problem worth raising.

problems.title: The deploy check refused three nights running over a file that is out of date by design — FIXED
problems.detail: Our deploy runs a check that our internal architecture map is up to date. Part of that check compared a generated web page (docs/architecture/index.html) against what the source would produce now — but that page is deliberately excluded from the project's saved files, so it only ever holds whatever the last person to run the generator locally produced. Merge somebody's work, pull it down, and the page is stale immediately and permanently. The check refused; regenerating cleared it while showing no change at all, which is what made it look like a ghost. Diagnosed at the artifacts by the previous shift, fixed here (#195): a freshness verdict is only a finding where there is a saved copy somebody could review. No customer effect at any point — the only cost was shift time, roughly half an hour a night for three nights.

problems.title: Quiet shifts were deploying — FIXED: the rite now refuses a briefing whose only change is a quiet journal line
problems.detail: Two quiet shifts this morning (09:45, 10:23) each ran a full production deploy for one journal line, after the standing orders had said a quiet shift ships nothing. The runner backs off 30 minutes after a quiet shift, and the deploy rite now refuses the quiet edition itself (PR #160) — so the order is a mechanical guard, not a sentence. No customer effect.
